entry.title: Violin Notes — 08 · Grade 8 Virtuoso Bowing, All Double Stops, Performance Polish
entry.content: Grade 8 ABRSM violin is the diploma threshold . All major and minor scales in three or four octaves, double stops in 3rds / 6ths / 8ves / 10ths, the full vocabulary of bow techniques (martelé, ricochet, sautillé, flying staccato, col legno , jeté ), and concerto / sonata repertoire approaching professional standard. Past Grade 8 lies DipABRSM and onward. Series map: 00 Beginner → 01 Grade 1 → … → 07 Grade 7 → 08 Grade 8 (this post — final in this series). Learning Outcome Play all major and minor three-octave scales + arpeggios fluently. Play scales in 3rds, 6ths, octaves, and 10ths in all common keys. Use every bow technique in repertoire. Apply expressive vibrato (variable speed + width) for musical effect. Perform a complete concerto movement of significant length (8–15 minutes) from memory. Read and interpret 20th-century notation (extended techniques, irregular metres). Demonstrate stylistic understanding: Baroque, Classical, Romantic, Modern. Chapter 1 — The full scale + double-stop arsenal Three-octave scales: every key By Grade 8 you must own all 12 major and all 12 minor (× 2 = harmonic + melodic) scales — three octaves each. Practice rotation (4-week cycle) Week Major keys Minor keys 1 C, G, D, A, E A, E, B, F♯, C♯ 2 B, F♯, C♯, D♭, A♭ G♯, D♯, A♯, B♭, F 3 E♭, B♭, F C, G, D 4 Review weakest 4 keys Review weakest 4 keys 15 minutes scales per day, rotating focus across the cycle. Double stops at Grade 8 Interval Difficulty Key example 3rds Moderate (Grade 6+) G, D, A major 6ths Moderate G, D, A major Octaves Hard G, D major 10ths Very hard Selected keys, single octave Fingered octaves Very hard Heifetz scale system 10ths require an enormous left-hand stretch (1st + 4th finger on adjacent strings, two octaves and a third apart). Most adult learners take 1–2 years to play 10ths reliably. Trick: don't force 10ths into pieces if they're not in the syllabus. Practise as a stretch exercise (open-palm yoga for the violin hand). When the syllabus demands them, you'll already have the reach. Chapter 2 — Virtuoso bowing toolkit By Grade 8 every technique is in active use. Quick reference: Bowing Description Typical use Détaché Smooth separate strokes Most Classical/Romantic passages Legato / slur Connected, one bow Lyrical lines Staccato Sharp short, on string Articulated passages Slurred staccato Multiple stops, one direction Long lines with articulation Spiccato Bow lifts between notes Light, dancing passages Sautillé Very fast spiccato Fast 16th-note passages Ricochet Multiple bounces per drop Showpieces, cadenzas Martelé Hammered, percussive Accents, dramatic openings Flying staccato Lifts each note, one direction Showpieces Col legno battuto Tap with the bow stick Modern repertoire, Mars (Holst) Col legno tratto Draw with the wood Eerie effects, rare Sul ponticello Near the bridge Glassy colour Sul tasto Over the fingerboard Soft, dreamy colour Pizzicato Plucked Common; Bartók pizz snaps string against fingerboard Jeté "Thrown" — multiple notes from a single bounce-then-draw Showpieces Tremolo Rapid bow oscillation on one note Suspense, orchestral effect A piece using nearly all of them Sarasate Zigeunerweisen uses détaché, legato, spiccato, sautillé, ricochet, harmonics, pizzicato, and flying staccato in one 9-minute work. Reference repertoire for technique synthesis. Chapter 3 — Vibrato as expression By Grade 8, vibrato is not "on" or "off" — it's a continuous parameter . The four vibrato variables Width — narrow (subtle warmth) vs wide (passionate Romantic). Speed — slow (sustained nobility) vs fast (intense, virtuoso fire). Continuous vs delayed — start the vibrato instantly, or let the note begin straight then add vibrato. Pulse — strict steady vibrato vs phrased vibrato (slows and speeds with the phrase). Vibrato style per period Period Vibrato preference Baroque Sparse, narrow, often as ornament (varies by historical performance practice) Classical Selective; on long notes mostly Romantic Continuous, wide, warm 20th-c / Modern Variable; sometimes deliberately senza vibrato Folk / world Narrow, fast, intermittent Trick: listen to one violinist play the same piece from different periods (e.g., Hilary Hahn plays both Bach and Tchaikovsky). Notice how her vibrato choice changes. Internalise the period-appropriate sound by daily listening. Chapter 4 — 20th-century notation Grade 8 introduces: Irregular metres 5/4, 7/8, 11/16. Count subdivisions: 1 2 3 4 5 / 4 = 3 + 2 or 2 + 3 7 / 8 = 2 + 2 + 3 or 3 + 2 + 2 11 / 16 = many possible groupings Listen: Holst Mars (5/4), Stravinsky Rite of Spring (constantly shifting metres). Extended techniques (notation symbols) Symbol Technique Diamond note Natural or artificial harmonic Open circle above note Natural harmonic "+" above note Left-hand pizzicato (pluck with left finger) "Bartók pizz" symbol Snap pluck (string against fingerboard) Wavy line above note Trill ↑ ↓ arrows Glissando direction Box around staff Aleatoric (player chooses) Atonal pitch language Some Grade 8 repertoire abandons traditional key signatures. Read by intervals, not by key. Practise by sight-reading short atonal exercises (Bartók Mikrokosmos arranged for violin, etc.). Chapter 5 — Suggested Performance Repertoire Concerto choices (Grade 8 level — pick one to focus 6 months) Concerto Composer Style Mozart Concerto No. 3, 4, or 5 Mozart Classical balance Bruch Concerto No. 1 in G minor Bruch Romantic favourite Saint-Saëns Concerto No. 3 in B minor Saint-Saëns French Romantic Mendelssohn Concerto in E minor Mendelssohn The "standard" Romantic Lalo Symphonie Espagnole Lalo Spanish-flavoured concerto Sonata choices Sonata Composer Style Bach Sonatas Nos. 1–3 (unaccompanied) Bach Baroque solo Beethoven Spring Sonata Op. 24 Beethoven Classical/early Romantic Brahms Sonatas 1, 2, 3 Brahms German Romantic Franck Sonata in A Franck Late Romantic French Showpieces (encore-level virtuoso) Piece Composer What it tests Zigeunerweisen Sarasate Every bowing technique Tzigane Ravel Harmonics, modal language Praeludium and Allegro Kreisler Pseudo-Baroque style Caprices (selected) Paganini Each caprice = one virtuoso problem Méditation from Thaïs Massenet Lyrical depth + vibrato Études at Grade 8 Rode 24 Caprices . Dont Op. 35 — major reference. Paganini 24 Caprices — start Nos. 5, 9, 13. Wieniawski L'École Moderne Op. 10. Chapter 6 — Performance polish Grade 8 exams test interpretation , not just technique. Programme planning (typical Grade 8 recital) Slot Choice Length 1 Baroque (Bach, Handel) 5–8 min 2 Classical / early Romantic (Mozart, Beethoven) 8–12 min 3 Late Romantic / Modern (Brahms, Ravel, Bartók) 5–10 min 4 Virtuoso showpiece 4–8 min Variety across periods is graded. Stage presentation Tuning ritual: walk onstage, tune visibly, take a breath, begin. Eye contact with pianist (if accompanied) before nodding to start. Bow direction visible to audience. Recovery: if you make a mistake, don't react . Continue. Audience usually misses small errors. Stage anxiety management Daily mock performance for 30 days before exam. Play full programme top-to-bottom every day. Performance-day routine : same warm-up, same meal timing, same clothing dress rehearsal. Breathing : 4 seconds in, 6 seconds out, before walking onstage. Lowers heart rate. Visualisation : mentally walk through the recital from arrival to bow, daily for 2 weeks before exam. Where I got stuck: I prepared technically but didn't rehearse the experience of performing. First exam: hands shook on the bow. Fix: 4 weeks of daily mock recitals — in front of family, friends, even an empty room with a recording running. By exam day, the room was less intimidating because I'd "performed" 30 times already. Chapter 7 — Stylistic understanding Grade 8 exams ask: Why is this Baroque ornament played this way? You should know: Baroque (1600–1750) Trills start on upper note , on the beat . Less vibrato; vibrato as occasional ornament. Strong terraced dynamics (sudden f to p, not gradual). Rubato sparingly; mostly steady tempo. Détaché with subtle weight changes for phrase shape. Classical (1750–1820) Balanced phrases, clear structure. Vibrato on long notes only. Dynamic gradients (cresc, dim) more frequent. Détaché with elegance; spiccato light. Romantic (1820–1900) Vibrato continuous. Wide dynamic range; rubato substantial. Long lyrical lines. Full use of register; expressive shifts welcomed. Modern (1900+) Technique-heavy. May use extended techniques. Senza vibrato on certain passages. Irregular metres + atonal pitch language possible. How to internalise style Listen to one piece per period weekly, with score in hand. Mark performance choices (vibrato, rubato, bowing). Compare across recordings. Over a year, style sensitivity becomes second nature. Chapter 8 — Aural / Listening Skills Grade 8 aural is extensive : Sing/play 8-bar phrases with modulations and chromatic notes after 1–2 hearings. Identify period + style at sight/sound. Identify formal structure (sonata-allegro, rondo, theme + variations). Identify modulations to distant + enharmonic keys. Identify orchestral textures (homophonic, polyphonic, monophonic). Sight-sing complex 8-bar phrases with modulation + chromaticism. Daily preparation 15 minutes ear training daily for 3 months before exam. Use Tonal Energy , Functional Ear Trainer , or Teoria.com drills. Mix: Intervals (target: 1 sec recognition) Chord qualities (target: 2 sec recognition) Modulation type (target: 5 sec recognition) Period style (target: 10 sec from short clip) Chapter 9 — Beyond Grade 8: the diploma path After Grade 8, the ABRSM diploma path: Diploma Level Requirements ARSM Performance diploma 30-min recital, professional standard DipABRSM Performance / Teaching 35-min recital + viva / pedagogy paper LRSM Licentiate 50-min recital + extensive theory FRSM Fellowship Concert-artist level Most adult learners stop at Grade 8 or ARSM. The leap to DipABRSM and beyond is substantial — concerto level reaches Tchaikovsky / Brahms / Sibelius standards, with full memorisation and stylistic mastery. Useful Shortcut Cheat-sheet What How All scales 3-octave + arpeggio + dom 7 + dim 7 Double stops 3rds + 6ths + 8ves + 10ths Full bow vocabulary Every technique in active use Vibrato Variable: width × speed × delay × pulse Memorisation Section + mental + random-start drill Period style Listen weekly; mark interpretive choices Performance 30-day mock recital before exam Beyond Grade 8 ARSM → DipABRSM → LRSM → FRSM Daily routine (150 min) Block Time Content Tune 3 min Tuner + 5ths Bow warm-up 12 min Full vocabulary cycle (8 bowings) Vibrato 5 min Variable width/speed on slow scale Scales (single notes) 15 min Rotating 3-octave + arpeggios + dom 7 Scales (double stops) 20 min 3rds + 6ths + 8ves + (10ths) Étude 20 min Rode / Dont / Paganini Sight-read 10 min 32-bar passage, atonal or modal mix Repertoire 1 30 min Main concerto movement Repertoire 2 20 min Sonata movement or showpiece Memory + mental 10 min Mental walkthrough + random-start Cool-down 5 min Slow scale, listen, release tension Suggested listening (context) Listen across periods. Each weekly listening: Period Reference recording Baroque Hilary Hahn — Bach Sonatas & Partitas Classical Anne-Sophie Mutter — Mozart Violin Concertos Romantic Itzhak Perlman — Tchaikovsky / Brahms / Mendelssohn Concertos 20th-c Maxim Vengerov — Shostakovich Concerto No. 1 Virtuoso Salvatore Accardo — Paganini 24 Caprices Modern Patricia Kopatchinskaja — Bartók / Ligeti Trick: every great violinist has a different sound. By Grade 8 you should start to hear "this is Hahn vs this is Mutter vs this is Perlman" within 5 seconds of a clip. That auditory sensitivity is what informs your own interpretive choices. Closing — the journey from Grade 1 Looking back across this series: Grades 1–2 : getting the hands to work at all. Grades 3–4 : first shift, first concerto, first real expression. Grade 5 : the bottleneck (vibrato + theory paper). Grades 6–7 : double stops, advanced bowings, full repertoire. Grade 8 : synthesis — every technique in service of musical interpretation. Grade 8 isn't an endpoint; it's a license to start the real study — the chamber music, the recital tours, the deeper Bach partitas, the modern works. Many adult learners find Grade 8 is where the violin finally feels like a voice rather than a project. Final trick: keep listening. Daily, lifelong. Every great violinist I admire spends more time listening than playing. Hearing shapes the hand. Hearing shapes the bow. Hearing makes you a musician — not just a violinist. References ABRSM (current). Violin Exam Pieces — Grade 8 . Carl Flesch, Scale System for Violin (complete). Heifetz, Heifetz Scale Book . Galamian, Contemporary Violin Technique . Simon Fischer, The Violin Lesson , Practice , Tone . Paganini, 24 Caprices Op. 1 . Rode, 24 Caprices . Dont, Op. 35. IMSLP — Bach Sonatas & Partitas, Mozart concertos, Mendelssohn, Bruch, Lalo, Saint-Saëns, Brahms, Franck. Note: this post — and this series — is in progress . entry.title: Violin Notes — 07 · Grade 7 All Positions, Harmonics, Advanced Bowing
entry.content: Grade 7 ABRSM violin is conservatory-entry territory . Every position from half to 8th is required, three-octave scales in all major and minor keys, harmonics (natural and artificial), more double-stop intervals (4ths, octaves), and the bow technique vocabulary expands to martelé , ricochet , sautillé . Repertoire is full Romantic concertos and Bach solo suite movements. Series map: 00 Beginner → 01 Grade 1 → … → 06 Grade 6 → 07 Grade 7 (this post) → 08 Grade 8. Learning Outcome Play all major and minor scales (three-octave + harmonic & melodic minor). Use all positions half through 8th in repertoire. Play natural harmonics and introduce artificial harmonics . Use martelé ("hammered"), ricochet ("thrown bow"), sautillé (fast spiccato). Play octaves as double stops in selected keys. Identify modulations to remote keys; understand modal music. Perform a complete Romantic concerto movement. Chapter 1 — Harmonics: the bell-like tones A harmonic is a high, pure, bell-like tone produced by lightly touching the string at specific nodes (rather than pressing down). Natural harmonics Found at division points of the open string: Touch point on string Resulting harmonic Pitch 1/2 (octave node) 1st overtone Open string + octave 1/3 node 2nd overtone Octave + 5th 1/4 node 3rd overtone Two octaves above open 1/5 node 4th overtone Two octaves + maj 3rd The 1/2 node on the A string is found by lightly touching with your 4th finger at the position where the 4th finger would normally play A5 (one octave above open A). The sound: a soft, ringing high A — an octave higher than expected. Trick: harmonics need almost no finger pressure — just a feather touch. If you press, you get a muted scratchy note. If you brush, you get the pure overtone. Practise the touch on open A: bow long stroke, feather-touch where the 4th finger sits in 1st position. The ringing high A appears almost magically. Artificial harmonics Press one finger firmly (the "stopping finger") and touch with another finger 1/4 above (the "harmonic finger"). The pitch produced is two octaves above the stopped pitch . 1 2 3 4 1 st finger: presses A on G string (= A4) 4 th finger: lightly touches D on G string (= 1 / 4 above ) sounding: A6 (two octaves above A4) Notation: diamond-shape note head for the touched note, plus regular note for the stopped note. Used famously in: Tchaikovsky Violin Concerto, Paganini Caprices, Ravel Tzigane . Chapter 2 — All positions: fluency target By Grade 7, you've learned half, 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 5th, 6th, 7th positions. Now: 8th position and fluency across all of them . 8th position On the A string: 1=B5, 2=C♯6, 3=D6, 4=E6 (right at the top of the violin's standard range for most pieces). The left hand pivots: thumb shifts to a different angle, hand approaches the bridge. The fluency goal You should be able to: Shift to any position without looking . Find the correct first finger pitch within a quarter-tone, on the first try. Choose appropriate position for expression (tone colour) — not just to reach a note. Trick: practise a single piece entirely in 1st position, then again entirely in 3rd, then entirely in 5th (skipping notes you can't reach). The same melody in different positions sounds different — different string vibrations, different timbre. Pick the position that suits the music . Position landmarks (physical) Position Hand landmark 1st Index touches the neck near the nut 3rd Thumb at the curve of the neck 5th Hand at the neck-body joint 7th Hand over the body curve 8th+ Thumb leaves the neck, sits on the shoulder of the violin Chapter 3 — Advanced bowings Martelé ("hammered") A short, percussive stroke with a strong attack and a dead stop. Bow pressure increased before the stroke begins, released through the stroke, stops abruptly. 1 2 [silent pressure build] → quick stroke → STOP → [silent pressure build] → next stroke Used for: marching feel, accented passages, opening of dramatic phrases. Ricochet ("rebound, thrown") Multiple notes from a single thrown bow . The bow is dropped from above, bounces 2–4 times naturally, lifted before it stops. 1 2 ↓ drop → bounce, bounce, bounce → lift Used in: Mendelssohn Concerto last movement, Paganini Caprices, Sarasate showpieces. Sautillé ("springing") Very fast spiccato — so fast that the bow no longer fully lifts off; the wood "springs" rapidly. Played in the middle of the bow with a loose grip. 1 2 ∾∾∾∾∾∾ at metronome 144 + per quaver Used in: Vivaldi Four Seasons (Summer storm), Beethoven Concerto 1st mvt, Mendelssohn Concerto 1st mvt. Where I got stuck: I couldn't transition from spiccato to sautillé. The hand wanted to "control" each bounce. Fix: extreme tempo experiment. Start a tremolo (very fast back-and-forth on one note). Gradually add finger changes. The wrist learns the bouncing speed first, then the fingers add pitches. Chapter 4 — Octave double stops Two notes an octave apart, played simultaneously. Fingering: 1st finger on lower string + 4th finger on upper string, 3 strings apart (e.g., 1 on G + 4 on D for an octave). Octaves require: 1st and 4th fingers to be exactly in tune with each other. 3rd and 4th fingers stretched apart maximally. Practice Slow tuner work. Tune 1st finger first; freeze it. Add 4th finger; adjust until the octave rings (no beats). Then bow the double stop. Practise on every string pair: G+D, D+A, A+E. Trick: octaves are the second-hardest interval to tune (after major 7ths). Beats are very audible; an octave that's even slightly off sounds painful. Practise daily for 5 minutes. Octave fluency takes 6 months minimum. Chapter 5 — Modulations to remote keys Grade 7 introduces modulation analysis to: Distant keys (e.g., C major → E major; 4 sharps' difference) Modal music (Dorian, Phrygian, Mixolydian, Lydian) Modal recognition Mode Built on (C major scale) Sound Ionian C — C Major (familiar) Dorian D — D Minor with raised 6 Phrygian E — E Minor with lowered 2 (Spanish/Flamenco) Lydian F — F Major with raised 4 (dreamy) Mixolydian G — G Major with lowered 7 (folk/rock) Aeolian A — A Natural minor Locrian B — B Diminished, rare Trick: listen to Bartók Romanian Folk Dances , Bach modal cantatas, Debussy. Modal music sounds "neither major nor minor". Train the ear to spot the characteristic interval that defines each mode (Dorian's raised 6, Phrygian's lowered 2, etc.). Chapter 6 — Suggested Practice Pieces Suzuki Vol. 7 staples Piece Composer Why Sonata No. 3 in F major Handel Full Baroque sonata, four movements Courante (Partita 3) Bach Bach solo, foundational Gigue (Partita 3) Bach Compound rhythm, Bach mastery Concerto in G minor Bach (BWV 1056 arr.) Bach concerto level ABRSM Grade 7 alternatives Piece Composer Why Concerto No. 4 in D, 1st mvt Mozart Standard Mozart concerto Concerto in E minor, 1st mvt Mendelssohn The Romantic concerto every violinist plays Méditation (full) Massenet Vibrato + harmonic showcase Romance in G Beethoven Mature Beethoven Sonata in A César Franck (excerpts) Late Romantic chamber Praeludium and Allegro Kreisler Style showpiece Étude staples Kreutzer — Nos. 12, 18, 30, 42 (the "famous" ones). Dont Op. 35 — opening. Rode 24 Caprices — first few. Chapter 7 — Memorisation strategy By Grade 7, you should perform from memory. Strategy: Analyse the structure first. Break the piece into sections (A-B-A, exposition-development-recap, theme + variations, etc.). Label each section. Memorise section by section — not start-to-finish. Memorise the hardest section first. Mental energy is highest at the start of practice; spend it on the toughest bars. Practise from any starting point. Open the score randomly; you should be able to start there from memory. This builds resilience for performance anxiety. Mental practice. Without the violin, mentally walk through the piece — every shift, every bow direction, every fingering. 10 minutes a day. Increases memory reliability dramatically. Slow performance practice. Once memorised, play the whole piece at 60% tempo from memory. Catches weak spots. Where I got stuck: I memorised by repetition only — fingers learned the piece, but my brain didn't. Under stress (an audition), my fingers blanked. Fix: 10 minutes of mental practice daily. It feels useless at first, but after a month, memory failure rate dropped 80%. Chapter 8 — Aural / Listening Skills Grade 7 aural: Sing/play 8-bar phrases with modulations after 2 hearings. Identify modes (Dorian, Phrygian, etc.). Identify chord progressions with non-diatonic chords. Sight-sing 8-bar with modulation. Identify period (Baroque / Classical / Romantic / 20th-c) by style. Chapter 9 — Common Grade 7 Pitfalls Pitfall Fix Harmonics fail (muted instead of ringing) Even lighter touch; check string is at exact node Octaves out of tune 5 min daily tuner work; tune one finger, freeze, add other Ricochet uneven bouncing Find balance point on bow; relax wrist; experiment with drop angle Sautillé loses speed mid-passage Increase metronome gradually over weeks; loose grip Memorisation fails in performance Mental practice daily; random-start-point drill Mode identification wrong Listen to canonical examples; sing the characteristic interval Bach Partita feels mechanical Listen to Hahn, Mutter, Heifetz versions; absorb style Useful Shortcut Cheat-sheet What How Natural harmonic Light touch at node points (1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5 of string) Artificial harmonic Press 1, touch 4 a 4th above; sound = 2 octaves above press 8th position Thumb leaves neck, hand near bridge Martelé Pressure build → stroke → stop Ricochet Drop bow, natural bounces, lift Sautillé Very fast spiccato, middle bow, loose grip Octaves 1 lower + 4 upper, exact tune Modes Each starts on different scale degree of major Memory strategy Section-by-section + mental practice + random-start Daily routine (120 min) Block Time Content Tune 3 min Tuner + 5ths Bow warm-up 10 min Long bows + spiccato + ricochet + sautillé drills Vibrato + tone 5 min Vibrato variety (slow / medium / fast) Scales (single notes) 15 min 2 three-octave + 2 minor (har + mel) Scales (double stops) 15 min 3rds + 6ths + octaves Chromatic + harmonics 5 min Chromatic up + harmonic drill Étude 15 min Kreutzer / Rode Sight-read 5 min New 24-bar passage Repertoire 35 min Full concerto movement, slow + tempo Memory work 7 min Mental practice + random-start drill Cool-down 5 min Slow scale, listen to tone Suggested listening (context) Piece Performer Why Mendelssohn Violin Concerto in E minor Anne-Sophie Mutter The Romantic concerto bar Bach Partita No. 3 in E major Hilary Hahn Bach Partita reference Tchaikovsky Violin Concerto Hahn Adult repertoire Brahms Violin Concerto Mutter German Romantic Ravel — Tzigane Sarah Chang Showcase for harmonics + every advanced technique Paganini — Caprices Nos. 5, 24 Salvatore Accardo Aspirational pinnacle References ABRSM (current). Violin Exam Pieces — Grade 7 . Suzuki, S. Suzuki Violin School , Vol. 7. Carl Flesch, Scale System . Kreutzer 42 Études , Dont Op. 35, Rode 24 Caprices . Simon Fischer, Tone and Practice . Galamian, Contemporary Violin Technique . IMSLP — Bach Sonatas & Partitas, Mendelssohn, Mozart concertos. Note: this post is in progress . entry.title: Violin Notes — 06 · Grade 6 Double Stops, Higher Positions, Chromatic Scales
entry.content: Grade 6 ABRSM violin is where the instrument doubles itself . Double stops — two strings sounded together — become a syllabus requirement. The right hand learns flying staccato, the left hand uses all positions through 5th regularly, and chromatic scales add 12-note fluency. The repertoire is now full Baroque sonatas, mid-Romantic showpieces, and the first complete concerto movements expected at concert level. Series map: 00 Beginner → 01 Grade 1 → … → 05 Grade 5 → 06 Grade 6 (this post) → 07 Grade 7 → 08 Grade 8. Learning Outcome Play 3rds and 6ths double stops through one octave on selected keys. Play chromatic scale (one or two octaves) starting on G or A. Use 1st–5th positions fluently in a single piece. Play three-octave scales in G, A, B♭ major (and some minor). Use staccato volante ("flying staccato") in showpieces. Identify ornaments + execute trills, mordents, turns idiomatically. Perform a complete sonata movement + a Romantic showpiece. Chapter 1 — Double stops: the violin singing in two voices A double stop is two strings bowed simultaneously, each producing a different pitch. The bow must contact both strings at once . Bow angle for double stops The bow normally tilts to one side to contact one string. For double stops, the bow lies flat on both strings at the same angle. Bow arm height adjusts to suit. Easy double stops: open string + stopped string Examples: Open D + 3rd finger A on D = A4 + D5 (a 4th) Open A + 1st finger B on E = B5 + open A (depends; usually combined notes) These are the entry-level double stops; you've been hearing them in pieces since Grade 3 (as the drone effect). Stopped double stops: 3rds Two fingers on adjacent strings, both stopped. For a 3rd in 1st position: 1 2 3 4 A string: 1 =B E string: 1 =F♯ sounding : B4 + F♯ 5 = a 5 th... wait, that's a 5 th To get a 3rd , you need adjacent fingers giving notes 3 letters apart. In 3rd position on A + E: 1 2 3 4 A string: 1 =D E string: 1 =F♯ sounding : D5 + F♯ 5 = a major 3 rd The Grade 6 syllabus typically asks for a one-octave scale in 3rds in keys like G major. 6ths 1 2 3 4 A string: 1 =B E string: 2 =G♯ sounding : B4 + G♯ 5 = a 6 th Two-finger spread; the two fingers are usually on different strings, one slightly behind the other. Where I got stuck: my fingers couldn't independently stop adjacent strings at different positions. Fix: very slow practice with a tuner on each note separately, then together. 5 minutes per day, 6 weeks, before any scale in 3rds was reliable. Chapter 2 — Chromatic scale 12 semitones in one octave, played either with traditional fingering or sliding-finger chromatic . Traditional fingering (G chromatic ascending, one octave on G + D string) 1 2 Open G → 1 =G♯ → 1 =A → 2 =A♯ → 2 =B → 3 =C → 4 =C♯ → open D .. . The same finger plays two consecutive semitones by sliding (1 plays G♯ then A; 2 plays A♯ then B). The finger slides up about ½ a finger-width. Galamian's chromatic fingering Uses a different finger pattern that avoids slides. Faster but harder to learn. Trick: the slide-finger chromatic is more idiomatic and what most pieces expect. Practise it very slowly with metronome. The "click" of the finger sliding between two semitones should be inaudible — the bow disguises it. Chapter 3 — Flying staccato ( staccato volante ) A series of bouncing staccato notes all on one bow direction , the bow lifting between each. 1 2 3 . . . . . . ↓ ♪ ♪ ♪ ♪ ♪ ♪ = 6 staccato notes on a single down-bow Distinct from slurred staccato (which stays on the string). Flying staccato lifts. How to learn it Solid up-bow staccato first (easier direction). 4 notes per bow at slow tempo. Each note: bow stops and lifts a millimetre , then drops for the next note. Build to 8 notes per bow. Reverse to down-bow staccato. Used famously in: Sarasate Zigeunerweisen , Wieniawski concertos, encore showpieces. Trick: the wrist + fingers produce the "stop+lift" motion; the arm stays steady. If your arm is jerking, you're forcing it. Relax, slow down. Chapter 4 — Higher positions: 6th, 7th, half position Half position The hand sits below 1st position — 1st finger plays where the open string normally sounds (or a semitone above). Used for low chromatic passages. 6th and 7th positions 6th pos on A: 1=G♯5. 7th pos on A: 1=A5 (an octave above open A). In 7th position, the hand sits over the body of the violin. Thumb adjusts to a different position; left hand has limited mobility. Used mostly for very high passages in concertos and showpieces. Where I got stuck: my left wrist collapsed in 7th position — the angle felt wrong. Fix: explicitly lift the left elbow forward (more underneath the violin) when shifting above 5th. The hand pivots more from underneath. Chapter 5 — Ornaments executed idiomatically Grade 6 demands playing , not just identifying, ornaments. Trill (tr or ⟵⟶) Rapid alternation between the written note and the note a step above . In Baroque: starts on the upper note. In Classical/Romantic: starts on the written note. 1 2 Trill on A4 : A B A B A B A B ... (very fast) The 2nd finger trills (lift-drop) while bow sustains. Trill speed: 6–10 oscillations per second. Practise slowly first, build speed. Mordent (𝆚) Quick three-note ornament: written note → step below (or above) → written note. 1 2 Lower mordent on A : A G A (very fast, takes maybe 1 / 8 of a beat) Turn (∾) Four-note ornament: above-note → written → below-note → written. 1 2 Turn on A : B A G A Appoggiatura (small note before main note) Takes half the value of the following note in Classical music. Acciaccatura (small note with slash through stem) A "crush" note — played as fast as possible, then immediately to the main note. Chapter 6 — Suggested Practice Pieces Suzuki Vol. 6 staples Piece Composer Why La Folia Corelli (arr. entry.title: Violin Notes — 05 · Grade 5 Vibrato, Shifting Across Positions, Three-Octave Scales
entry.content: Grade 5 ABRSM violin is the milestone exam. Pass it, and you've earned the right to attempt Grades 6–8 (which require Grade 5 theory as a prerequisite — read your local rules). Technically, Grade 5 demands vibrato , shifts to 4th and 5th position , the first three-octave scales for some keys, and a far wider repertoire including full sonata movements. Series map: 00 Beginner → 01 Grade 1 → … → 04 Grade 4 → 05 Grade 5 (this post) → 06 Grade 6 → 07 Grade 7 → 08 Grade 8. Learning Outcome Apply continuous vibrato to sustained notes. Shift fluently between 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, and 5th positions. Play three-octave G and A major scales (some syllabi). Play two-octave scales in all major keys + most minor keys (harmonic + melodic). Use sul G (play on G string only) and sul ponticello / sul tasto colour techniques. Identify all triads (major, minor, diminished, augmented) at sight. Play a complete Baroque sonata movement + one concerto movement. Chapter 1 — Vibrato: the expression Vibrato is the small, rapid pitch oscillation that adds warmth and life to sustained notes. Without it, classical violin tone sounds naked . Three vibrato types Type Source Speed When Wrist vibrato Wrist rocks back and forth Medium Most repertoire Arm vibrato Whole forearm rocks Slow + wide Romantic, big tone Finger vibrato Finger joint flexes Fast + narrow Rare; modern works Wrist is the standard first vibrato taught at Grade 5. Learning wrist vibrato — step by step Air vibrato — without violin. Hold left arm up as if holding violin. Wave hand at the wrist, palm-up to palm-down motion, for 30 sec. This is the motion. Vibrato on knee. Sit. Place finger on knee. Rock wrist gently, finger stays in contact, pad rolls. Build motor pattern. Vibrato on violin neck (no string). Finger on the neck, not string. Rock wrist. Vibrato on string with finger anchored. 3rd finger on A (= D5). Bow long open D. Rock wrist; finger should roll (not slide). Pitch should wobble below the pitch and back to it. Slow metronome vibrato. 4 wobbles per beat at 60 bpm = 4 Hz. Build to 6 Hz over 6 months. Apply to scales. Vibrate every sustained note in a slow scale. Where I got stuck: my wrist locked. Vibrato felt impossible for 3 months. Fix: spend 5 minutes per day on the "knee drill" — no violin, no string, just the wrist motion. The brain learns motion separately from instrument. Once the wrist could rock freely, transferring to the violin took one week. Pitch direction Vibrato should wobble below the in-tune pitch back up to it . Never above . The brain hears the upper limit of the oscillation as "the note". Where to start using it Don't vibrate every note. Start with: Long notes (half-notes, whole-notes). Phrase peak notes. Final note of a phrase. By Grade 6, you'll vibrate almost every note that's longer than a quaver. At Grade 5, just the obvious ones. Chapter 2 — Shifting to 4th and 5th positions 4th position On the A string: 1=E5, 2=F♯5, 3=G♯5, 4=A5. Note: 4 in 4th position = A5 = open E next door. Useful for staying on one string. 5th position 1=F♯5, 2=G♯5, 3=A5, 4=B5. 5th position is where the violin's neck meets the body . The thumb position changes — you'll start using the "shoulder" of the violin as a reference. The shift map (3-octave G major) To play G major across 3 octaves, you traverse: G string: 1st position G-A-B-C D string: 1st pos D-E-F♯-G A string: 1st pos A-B-C♯-D E string: 1st pos E-F♯-G Shift to 3rd pos on E : A-B-C Shift to 5th pos on E : D-E (or shift higher: 7th position D-E-F♯-G — depends on edition) Trick: learn the shift route as a fixed sequence. Mark "III" or "V" above the music. Practise just the route (no rhythm) until the shifts are automatic; then add timing. Silent shift drill (essential at Grade 5+) Bow open A. Slide 1st finger up to D5 (3rd pos). Continue sliding to F♯5 (5th pos). Back down to D5, then to 1st position B. Repeat 10×, very slowly. No glissando audible. Daily. The shifts smoothen over weeks. Chapter 3 — Three-octave scales The standard 3-octave scale layout (G major shown): 1 2 3 4 5 6 G string: G A B C ( 1 st position, fingers 0 - 1 - 2 - 3 ) D string: D E F♯ G ( 1 st position, fingers 0 - 1 - 2 - 3 ) A string: A B C♯ D ( 1 st position, fingers 0 - 1 - 2 - 3 ) E string: E F♯ G A ( 1 st pos: 0 - 1 - 2 - 3 ) E string: B C D E G (shift to 3 rd pos: 1 - 2 - 3 - 4 ... then shift again) Exact fingering varies by teacher. Pick one fingering and stick to it for 6 months minimum. Switching fingerings mid-learning resets your muscle memory. Recommended fingering source Carl Flesch, Scale System — the bible of violin scales. Used by every conservatory student. Galamian Contemporary Violin Technique — slightly different fingerings. Whichever your teacher prefers. Chapter 4 — Triads: all four qualities Grade 5 theory requires identification of: Triad Intervals (from root) Sound Major Maj 3rd + Min 3rd Bright Minor Min 3rd + Maj 3rd Sad Diminished Min 3rd + Min 3rd Tense, unstable Augmented Maj 3rd + Maj 3rd Suspenseful, dreamy Building each from C C major: C–E–G (M3 + m3) C minor: C–E♭–G (m3 + M3) C diminished: C–E♭–G♭ (m3 + m3) C augmented: C–E–G♯ (M3 + M3) Inversions A triad has 3 notes; any of them can be in the bass: Position Bass note Example (C major) Root Root C–E–G First inversion 3rd E–G–C Second inversion 5th G–C–E Notation: figured bass uses ⁶ (1st inv) and ⁶⁄₄ (2nd inv). At Grade 5 you must identify these from a score. Chapter 5 — Tone colours Grade 5 introduces colour markings in scores. Common ones: Marking Italian Effect sul G "on the G string" Forces phrase onto G string for rich, dark tone sul D / A / E "on the D/A/E string" Same idea, different colour sul ponticello "near the bridge" Glassy, eerie, metallic sul tasto "over the fingerboard" Soft, flute-like, dreamy pizzicato "plucked" Plucked string col legno "with the wood" Tap with the bow stick Practise: D major scale sul ponticello , then sul tasto . The difference is dramatic. Composers exploit this. Chapter 6 — Suggested Practice Pieces Suzuki Vol. 5 staples Piece Composer Why Concerto in G minor Vivaldi Substantial concerto, multiple movements Gavotte J.B. Lully Baroque dance suite entry Country Dance C.M. von Weber Folk feel, dotted rhythms Concerto No. 5 in D, 1st mvt Vivaldi First major D-major concerto ABRSM Grade 5 alternatives Piece Composer Why Concerto in A minor, 1st mvt Accolay Standard student-concerto favourite Sonata in E minor Telemann Full Baroque sonata movement Romance Beethoven (excerpt) Lyrical, vibrato showcase Hungarian Dance Brahms (arr.) Rubato + folk fire Méditation from Thaïs Massenet (excerpt) The dream piece; finally playable Étude staples Wohlfahrt Op. 45 Book 2 — continued. Mazas Op. 36 Book 1 — étude graduation. Kreutzer 42 Études — start the first 5 by Grade 5. Chapter 7 — Aural / Listening Skills Grade 5 aural is a separate exam paper in some syllabi or a section of the practical. It includes: Sing or play back a 4–8 bar phrase after one hearing. Identify modulations to dominant or relative minor. Identify cadences in context. Identify chord progressions (basic I-IV-V-I). Sight-sing a longer phrase with leaps. Trick: daily aural drill. 5 minutes, every day. Apps: Tonal Energy , Functional Ear Trainer , Teoria . Random intervals → cadences → progressions → modulations. Build the ear like a muscle. Chapter 8 — The Grade 5 Theory prerequisite In the ABRSM system, you cannot enter the Grade 6, 7, or 8 practical exam without first passing Grade 5 Theory . This is the bottleneck. Grade 5 theory paper covers All intervals (size + quality, simple + compound). All triads (4 qualities + inversions). All cadences. Time signatures including 5/4, 7/8 (irregular). Transposition (writing music in a new key). Score reading (alto + tenor clefs introduction; full score interpretation). Composition: 8-bar melody using given opening. Ornament identification (trill, mordent, turn, appoggiatura, acciaccatura). Preparation strategy Buy ABRSM Music Theory in Practice — Grade 5 workbook. Work through 1 chapter per week. Take 2 past papers per month for the last 3 months. Aim for 90% on practice papers before booking the exam. Average study time: 6 months alongside violin practice. Chapter 9 — Common Grade 5 Pitfalls Pitfall Fix Vibrato sounds forced Slower metronome, focus on relaxation Shift to 5th pos misses by a semitone Slow silent shifts; visualise the position landmarks 3-octave scale fingers tangle Stick to ONE fingering; don't switch mid-week Triad confusion (major vs minor) Sing them; bottom 3rd = the giveaway Theory paper rushed Take past papers under timed conditions early Vibrato applied too aggressively to fast notes Apply only to long notes at first; speed will follow sul G phrase scratches at low end Bow weight + slow speed; G string demands patience Useful Shortcut Cheat-sheet What How Vibrato motion Wrist rocks; finger rolls below pitch back to it Vibrato start Knee drill → no-string → string anchored → bowed 4th position 1st finger E (A string) 5th position 1st finger F♯ (A string) 3-octave G major shifts Around E string upper octave Triad qualities Maj=M3+m3, Min=m3+M3, Dim=m3+m3, Aug=M3+M3 sul G Stay on G string for tone Grade 5 theory needed Required for Grade 6+ practical entry Daily routine (75 min) Block Time Content Tune 2 min Tuner + 5ths Bow warm-up 8 min Long bows + spiccato + colour drills Vibrato drill 5 min Slow on long notes Scales 15 min 1 three-octave + 2 two-octave (major + minor) Shifting drill 5 min Silent shifts up to 5th position Étude 10 min Wohlfahrt / Mazas Sight-read 5 min New piece Repertoire 20 min Concerto + sonata movement Cool-down 5 min Slow vibrato on open string-derived pitch Suggested listening (context) Piece Performer Why Vivaldi Four Seasons Itzhak Perlman Standard violin repertoire; many Grade 5–7 segments Mozart Violin Sonata K. 304 in E minor Hahn The "tragic" sonata; mature Mozart Bach Partita No. 2 — Chaconne Hilary Hahn Pinnacle solo violin; aspirational Brahms Violin Concerto Anne-Sophie Mutter Adult-career repertoire; listen for vibrato variety Sibelius Violin Concerto Hahn or Mutter The "rich, dark" tone goal References ABRSM (current). entry.title: Violin Notes — 04 · Grade 4 2nd & 3rd Position, Melodic Minor, Spiccato
entry.content: Grade 4 ABRSM violin is where the left hand finally leaves first position . Real 2nd and 3rd position shifting becomes required, melodic minor enters the playing syllabus, more flat/sharp keys (E♭, E, A♭) appear, and the right hand learns spiccato — the controlled bouncing bow. The repertoire moves into early concertos and substantial Baroque sonatas. Series map: 00 Beginner → 01 Grade 1 → 02 Grade 2 → 03 Grade 3 → 04 Grade 4 (this post) → 05 Grade 5 → … → 08 Grade 8. Learning Outcome Play two-octave scales in all keys up to 3 sharps and 3 flats majors. Play melodic minor in playing form (not just paper). Shift cleanly to 2nd and 3rd position and back. Begin spiccato (controlled bouncing bow) on open strings + simple scales. Identify all interval qualities at sight. Play 6–8 Grade 4 pieces including one early concerto movement. Chapter 1 — Position shifting becomes routine 3rd position — the workhorse 3rd position is the second most used position after 1st. Most professional violinists spend 60–70% of playing time in 1st or 3rd. Finding 3rd position On the A string: Play open A. Slide 1st finger up until it sounds D5 (the same pitch as 3rd finger in 1st position). Now: 1=D5, 2=E5, 3=F♯5 (in D major), 4=G5. Other strings analogous: G string: 1=C, 2=D, 3=E (depending on key), 4=F or F♯. D string: 1=G, 2=A, 3=B (or B♭), 4=C. E string: 1=A, 2=B, 3=C♯ (or C), 4=D. The shift motion Three components, in this order: Release finger pressure (don't lift the finger — just release the press). Thumb and hand travel together up the neck. Press the new finger at the target. The finger that leads the shift is called the guide finger . In a 1→3 shift, the guide is whichever finger is currently down — usually 1. Trick: practise silent shifts. Bow open string, shift the left hand up and down while the bow drones the open string. You should hear no glissando — only the open string ringing. If you hear a "scrape", the guide finger is pressing too hard during the slide. 2nd position Less common than 3rd. The hand sits halfway between 1st and 3rd. On the A string: 1=C♯/C, 2=D, 3=E, 4=F♯/F. 2nd position is the answer when a phrase sits just above 1st position but doesn't go high enough to need 3rd. Used for awkward fingerings, not new pitches. How to choose position Reason Position to use Reach high notes Higher position Stay on same string (tone colour) Whatever position keeps you there Avoid awkward string crossing The position that smooths the line Score marks it Composer chose; obey Difficult fingering pattern Try 2nd position Chapter 2 — Melodic minor in playing Grade 3 introduced melodic minor on paper. Grade 4 requires playing. D melodic minor (one or two octaves) Ascending: D E F G A B C♯ D — raise 6 (B) and 7 (C♯). Descending: D C B♭ A G F E D — back to natural. Fingering (one octave on D + A): 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 Ascending: D string: D 1 =E 2 =F 3 =G A string: A 1 =B(normal pos) 2 =C♯ 3 =D Descending: A string: D 2 =C 1 =B♭(low!) A D string: 3 =G 2 =F 1 =E D That B♭ on descent / B♮ on ascent on the same string is the tricky part. Same finger (1), different position. Where I got stuck: my hand could not switch B♮ ↔ B♭ in one scale. Fix: bow only the A string portion (B♭ down, B♮ up) until the finger shape change became automatic. Don't add the rest of the scale until that bar is reliable. All Grade 4 minors Minor Form Octaves D minor Harmonic + Melodic 2 G minor Harmonic + Melodic 1 (some 2) A minor Harmonic + Melodic 2 E minor Harmonic + Melodic 1 or 2 Six combinations to practise. Allocate one minor per day, rotate. Chapter 3 — Spiccato: the controlled bounce Spiccato is the foundation of all advanced bowing. The bow lifts off the string between notes — not because you lifted it, but because the bow's elasticity bounces it. How spiccato works The bow is flexible . When dropped onto the string and pulled, the wood + hair vibrate vertically — they want to bounce. Find the "sweet spot" (middle to slightly upper-middle of the bow), drop with just enough weight, draw a short stroke, and the bow rebounds for the next note. Spiccato practice progression Drop test. Hold the bow over the A string, let it fall from 1 cm above, watch it bounce. Find the bow position where bounce is most controlled (usually 4–6 inches above the middle, near the balance point). One bounce per drop. Drop, lift, drop. Slow. Two bounces per drop without re-lifting. The bow bounces itself. Continuous bouncing on open string at metronome 60. Add scale notes. D major scale, spiccato. Speed up gradually to 100, then 120. Trick: spiccato fails when you grip the bow. Relax thumb + pinky; let the bow do the work. If your wrist hurts after spiccato practice, you're forcing it. Stop, shake out, restart looser. Détaché vs spiccato vs staccato — quick distinction Bowing Bow contact Sound Détaché On string Smooth separation Spiccato Bounces off Light, dancing Staccato On string, sharp stop Short, dry Slurred staccato On string, multiple stops one direction Pulsed long line Chapter 4 — New keys: E major, A♭ major E major (4 sharps: F♯ C♯ G♯ D♯) 1 2 3 E string: E 1 =F♯ 2 =G♯ 3 =A 4 =B A string: A(open) → continues up Fingering: normal "high" positions everywhere. Coming after the flat keys, E major feels easy because the violin's open strings (E, A, D) are all natural to the key. A♭ major (4 flats: B♭ E♭ A♭ D♭) The hardest playable key at Grade 4. Two "low" fingers on most strings; A♭ itself (instead of open A) creates an unusual hand position. Most editions require A♭ for one octave only at Grade 4. Two-octave A♭ is Grade 5+. Trick: don't memorise A♭ note-by-note. Memorise it as a modified D major shape , with low 1 on the D string and a low everywhere else. Pattern recognition over note recall. Chapter 5 — All four cadences (theory) Grade 4 paper requires recognition of all four cadences: Cadence Chords Sound Example Perfect (Authentic) V → I "Full stop" End of Twinkle Plagal ("Amen") IV → I "Settled, churchy" "Amen" at hymn end Imperfect (Half) any → V "Hanging question" Mid-phrase pause Interrupted V → vi (instead of I) "Surprise" Romantic deception Identify by ear in aural: play tonic chord + the cadence chord. Listen to the resolution. Trick: sing "Happy Birthday" — the last two chords are V → I , perfect. Sing the church "Amen" at the end of any hymn — that's IV → I , plagal. Pre-load these references; any cadence question becomes "which of my references does this match?". Chapter 6 — Suggested Practice Pieces Suzuki Vol. 4 staples Piece Composer Why Concerto in A minor, 1st movement Vivaldi The Suzuki 4 capstone; first real concerto Concerto No. 2 in G, 3rd movement Vivaldi Companion concerto, brighter mood Bourrée (from Lute Suite) Bach Compound rhythm + cross-string slurs Perpetual Motion Bohm Speed étude Largo Vivaldi Slow movement; vibrato preparation ABRSM Grade 4 alternatives Piece Composer Why Sonata in G Telemann Baroque sonata structure Tambourin Gossec Famous staccato show piece Andante Mozart Singing Classical line Hungarian Dance No. 5 Brahms (arr.) Folk fire; rubato test Vivaldi Concerto in A minor: a deeper note The first movement is the first concerto every Suzuki violinist plays . It includes: Energetic 16th-note passages A cadenza-like solo break Sequences (repeating patterns at different pitches) Multiple shifts to 3rd position A sense of dialogue between soloist and orchestra Practise this slowly: 4 weeks at half tempo before any attempt at performance speed. Chapter 7 — Aural / Listening Skills Grade 4 adds: Sing back a 4-bar phrase with one or two leaps. Identify cadences (perfect, plagal, imperfect, interrupted). Identify features in a passage (modulation? change of texture?). Sight-sing a simple 4-bar phrase (Grade 4+ feature). Sight-singing strategy Look at the time signature + key signature. Hum the tonic note (the examiner gives it). Trace the contour with your finger silently. Sing slowly with the rhythm correct. Don't worry about perfect pitch — relative shape matters more than absolute tuning at Grade 4. Chapter 8 — Common Grade 4 Pitfalls Pitfall Fix Shift sounds like a glissando Lighter thumb; silent practice Spiccato sounds scratchy Relax grip; find the right bow spot Melodic minor uses harmonic form descending Mark "natural here ↓" in score for first month A♭ major scale fingers slip Pattern memorise (low/normal map) rather than note-name Vivaldi tempo too fast too soon Half tempo for 2 weeks, ¾ for 1 week, full only week 4 Bow arm exhausted by spiccato Spiccato is wrist + finger, not arm. Drop arm tension Position guess wrong Pencil-mark "III" or "II" above first note of every shifted passage Useful Shortcut Cheat-sheet What How 3rd position 1st finger Plays what 3rd-finger plays in 1st pos Shift mechanics Release pressure → travel → press new finger Melodic minor Up: raise 6+7. Down: natural Spiccato sweet spot Middle to slightly upper-middle of bow E major "Easy" — all open strings are natural in key A♭ major Hardest Grade 4 key; pattern recognition Perfect cadence V → I — "full stop" Plagal cadence IV → I — "Amen" Imperfect cadence ... → V — "question" Interrupted cadence V → vi — "surprise" Daily routine (60 min) Block Time Content Tune 2 min Tuner + 5ths Bow warm-up 7 min Long bows + spiccato drill on open A Scales 15 min 2 major + 2 minor (har + mel) two-octave Shifting drill 5 min Silent shift 1↔3 on each string Études 8 min Wohlfahrt or Kayser study Sight-read 5 min New piece Repertoire 16 min Vivaldi concerto or current piece Cool-down 2 min Slow open string, listen to tone Suggested listening (context) Piece Performer Why Vivaldi A minor Concerto Anne-Sophie Mutter or Itzhak Perlman The piece you're learning, played pro Bach Double Concerto in D minor Hahn + Lara St. John Future repertoire (Grade 5–6) Mozart Violin Concerto No. 3 in G Anne-Sophie Mutter Standard concerto life-goal Sarasate — Zigeunerweisen Sarah Chang Spiccato showcase + Romantic fire Paganini — Caprice No. 24 Salvatore Accardo Pinnacle of bow technique; aspirational References ABRSM (current). entry.title: Violin Notes — 03 · Grade 3 New Keys, Shifting Prep & Slurred Staccato
entry.content: Grade 3 ABRSM violin is the gateway between "beginner who can play tunes" and "real student". Two new flat keys appear (B♭ and E♭), the three minor scales must be distinguished, a hint of position shifting is introduced, and bowings begin to diversify (slurred staccato, hooked bowing). The repertoire shifts toward Baroque dances and early Classical pieces. Series map: 00 Beginner → 01 Grade 1 → 02 Grade 2 → 03 Grade 3 (this post) → 04 Grade 4 → … → 08 Grade 8. Learning Outcome Play two-octave scales of G, D, A, B♭ majors and one-octave E♭ major. Play D, G, A natural and harmonic minors (one or two octaves as syllabus). Distinguish the three minor forms by ear and on paper. Use slurred staccato and hooked bowing . Prepare for 3rd position shifting (theoretical introduction). Identify interval quality (major, minor, perfect) at sight. Play 5–7 Grade 3 pieces with confident phrasing. Chapter 1 — B♭ major (two octaves) B♭ has two flats: B♭ and E♭. Translated to violin fingering: 1 2 3 4 5 G string: G 1 =A 2 =B♭(low 2!) 3 =C D string: D 1 =E♭(low 1!) 2 =F 3 =G A string: A 1 =B♭(low 1!) 2 =C 3 =D E string: E 1 =F 2 =G 3 =A Wait — that's three "low" fingers across the scale. The hand shape changes per string. Trick: the rule for any key with flats: drop the finger that plays the flatted note half a finger-width toward the nut. For B♭ major, that's 2 on G string, 1 on D, 1 on A. Memorise the pattern of which finger is low , not the abstract scale. Top note: B♭5 (4th finger on E in 1st position). Why this key matters B♭ is the first key violinists genuinely struggle with . The hand has to relearn its default spacing. Master B♭ by Grade 3, and every flat key after becomes intuitive. Chapter 2 — E♭ major (one octave) E♭ has three flats: B♭, E♭, A♭. One octave only at Grade 3. 1 2 3 4 D string: 3 =G (start position: 3rd finger E♭? Most editions start on E♭ on D string) A string: 1 =B♭(low) 2 =C 3 =D♭? — varies E string: 1 =E♭? — usually only goes to B♭5 max Different editions fingerprint this differently. The point: 3 flats means 3 "low" finger placements. Get the pattern of lowness right and your fingers will land. Where I got stuck: I tried to memorise E♭ as "B♭, E♭, A♭" abstractly. Fix: I stopped naming the flats and just thought "low-low-low" in the right places. Faster, more reliable. Chapter 3 — The three minor forms Grade 2 introduced natural minor . Grade 3 adds harmonic and (sometimes) melodic . Natural minor (review) Same notes as the relative major. A natural minor: 1 2 A B C D E F G A Harmonic minor — raises the 7th The leading-tone effect that classical music expects: 1 2 A B C D E F G ♯ A That raised 7th creates an augmented 2nd between F and G♯ (3 semitones — a full step + half-step). This gives harmonic minor its Middle-Eastern or Spanish flavour. Trick: harmonic minor sounds exotic compared to natural minor. Sing both ascending — natural feels "modal/folk", harmonic feels "classical/dramatic". After ten A/B comparisons, your ear locks the difference. Melodic minor — raises 6th and 7th going up, naturals coming down 1 2 3 Ascending : A B C D E F ♯ G ♯ A Descending : A G F E D C B A Two different note sets in one scale. Composers chose this in the Baroque to handle melodic lines without the harmonic minor's augmented 2nd "bump". Grade 3 typically requires melodic minor only on paper; full playing comes Grade 4. D, G, A minor (Grade 3 syllabus) Major Relative minor Common form examined F major D natural & harmonic minor Both B♭ major G natural & harmonic minor Both C major A natural & harmonic minor Both Practise: play the major scale, then immediately its relative minor (natural form). Then play harmonic minor of the same root. Six versions per session. Chapter 4 — Slurred staccato A new bowing. Notation: slur (curved line) + dot under each note within the slur. 1 2 3 . . . . ♪‿♪‿♪‿♪ = play 4 notes in one bow, but each separated by a tiny pause The bow stays on the string; the wrist makes a small stop-start motion for each note while moving in one direction. Where I got stuck: I lifted the bow between notes — that's staccato volante (flying staccato), Grade 6 stuff. Fix: practise on open strings, bow stays on the string, only the wrist pulses. Picture a bow that "hesitates" 4 times in one stroke. Hooked bowing Two unequal notes (often dotted-quaver + semiquaver) on one bow with a tiny stop between them: 1 2 ♪. 𝅘𝅥𝅯 <-- both on down- bow, stop between them Used to keep the dotted figure on the same bow direction throughout a phrase. Saves bow-direction confusion. Chapter 5 — Shifting: a theoretical preview True shifting (moving the hand to 2nd/3rd/etc. positions) is Grade 4 territory, but Grade 3 introduces the concept and may use one shift in a piece or as a "step out" of 1st position. Why shift? Reach higher notes the 1st position can't. Stay on one string for a phrase (changing tone colour). Make awkward fingerings easier. What 3rd position feels like In 3rd position, the 1st finger plays what the 3rd finger plays in 1st position . So on the A string: 1st position: 3rd finger = D5. 3rd position: 1st finger = D5. The hand moves up the neck by about 1 inch. First shift exercise On the A string: Open A, then 3rd finger D (1st position). Slide the 1st finger up the string until it sounds D. Now you're in 3rd position. Play 2 (E) and 3 (F♯). Don't lift; slide smoothly. The thumb travels with the hand. Trick: the thumb moves at the same time as the fingers. If the thumb stays back, you get a stretched, painful hand. Practise the shift with eyes closed, only feeling the smooth slide. Listen for the slide pitch — at first it'll glissando, later it'll be silent. Grade 3 may include one piece with a marked shift; Grade 4 requires the technique. Chapter 6 — Interval quality Grade 2 named interval size (2nd, 3rd, etc.). Grade 3 adds quality : Interval Semitones Example (from C) Perfect 1st (unison) 0 C–C Minor 2nd 1 C–D♭ Major 2nd 2 C–D Minor 3rd 3 C–E♭ Major 3rd 4 C–E Perfect 4th 5 C–F Tritone (Aug 4 / dim 5) 6 C–F♯ Perfect 5th 7 C–G Minor 6th 8 C–A♭ Major 6th 9 C–A Minor 7th 10 C–B♭ Major 7th 11 C–B Perfect 8ve 12 C–C (high) The 5 "perfect" intervals + 6 major/minor pairs + tritone Perfect : 1st, 4th, 5th, 8ve. Stable, "pure" sound. Major / minor : 2nd, 3rd, 6th, 7th. Have two flavours. Tritone : unstable, called diabolus in musica historically. Trick: the song hooks for intervals — sing the first two notes: Major 2nd: "Happy Birthday" ("Happy") Minor 3rd: "Greensleeves" ("A-las") Major 3rd: "When the Saints" ("Oh when") Perfect 4th: "Here Comes the Bride" Perfect 5th: "Twinkle, Twinkle" ("Twinkle") Minor 6th: "The Entertainer" ("ta-ta") Major 6th: "My Bonnie" Octave: "Somewhere Over the Rainbow" ("Some-where") Memorise one song per interval; identify intervals in 1 second. Chapter 7 — Suggested Practice Pieces Suzuki Vol. 3 staples Piece Composer Why Gavotte from Mignon A. Listen to Janine Jansen or Hilary Hahn play any Bach Partita gavotte. Notice how the dance accent (beat 3 of 4/4) is felt rather than punched. Chapter 8 — Aural / Listening Skills Grade 3 aural expands to: Sing back a 4–5 note phrase (more contour). Identify major / minor / chromatic. Identify key features: same, different, or modified (transposition or change in dynamics). Clap rhythms with dotted figures. Pitch matching pressure-test The examiner plays a note on the piano in a key you haven't been told. You must identify it and play it on the violin. Practise daily for 30 seconds; by Grade 3 exam, you should pick the right string + finger 90% of the time within 5 seconds. entry.title: Violin Notes — 02 · Grade 2 Two-Octave Scales & Slur Control
entry.content: Grade 2 ABRSM violin doubles your reach: two-octave scales, the first minor key, dotted rhythms, and longer slurs that demand real bow planning. The hand shape from Grade 1 stays, but it now travels — string crossings within a scale become the central skill. Series map: 00 Beginner → 01 Grade 1 → 02 Grade 2 (this post) → 03 Grade 3 → … → 08 Grade 8. Learning Outcome Play two-octave scales of G and D major, one-octave C and F major. Play A natural minor (one octave) and recognise the relative-minor concept. Use dotted-quaver + semiquaver rhythms accurately. Slur 4–8 notes per bow with even tone. Read fluently up to top D / E above the staff (E string, 4th finger). Play 4–6 Grade 2 pieces with hands together, musically shaped. Chapter 1 — Two-octave scales arrive A two-octave scale spans two strings (Grade 1 used two strings for one octave); now you traverse three strings. G major (two octaves) 1 2 3 4 5 G string: G 1 =A 2 =B 3 =C D string: D 1 =E 2 =F♯ 3 =G A string: A 1 =B 2 =C♯ 3 =D E string: E 1 =F♯ 2 =G ( no 3 needed; top note is G5 in many syllabi, or continue to A5 with 3rd finger) Grade 2 typically asks for the scale to reach G5 (3rd finger on E in 1st position). Some editions extend to A5. D major (two octaves) 1 2 3 4 D string: D 1 =E 2 =F♯ 3 =G A string: A 1 =B 2 =C♯ 3 =D E string: E 1 =F♯ 2 =G♯ 3 =A Top note is A5. C major (one octave) — first piece with no sharps 1 2 3 4 G string: 3 =C D string: D 1 =E 2 =F 3 =G ← half-step between 1 and 2 here! A string: A 1 =B 2 =C Trick: C major is the shock key for violin beginners. Every other scale you've played has the half-step between 2 and 3. C major has it between 1 and 2 on the D string. Mark the music with an arrow over the F natural for the first 2 weeks. F major (one octave) 1 2 3 4 D string: 3 =F ( or open F substitute on some editions) A string: A 1 =B♭ 2 =C 3 =D E string: E 1 =F 2 =G Half-step lands between finger 1 and 2 on the A string (B♭ → C). The B♭ requires placing finger 1 low — closer to the nut than normal. Where I got stuck: "low 1" felt unnatural for weeks. The finger wants to land where it always does. Fix: physically mark a tape line for "low 1" position on the A string for one practice session. Once your finger learns the distance, peel the tape off. Chapter 2 — The first minor scale: A natural minor A natural minor uses the same notes as C major but starts on A: 1 2 A B C D E F G A Fingering (one octave starting from open A): 1 2 3 A string: A 1 =B 2 =C 3 =D E string: E 1 =F 2 =G (3 not needed for one octave to A — use harmonic A) Or starting on the G string for low-octave practice: 1=A (low) ... but Grade 2 starts on open A. What "natural minor" means Three forms of minor exist: Form Pattern (intervals) Where used Natural W-H-W-W-H-W-W Grade 2 introduction Harmonic Raises 7th by half-step Grade 3+ Melodic Raises 6th + 7th going up, naturals coming down Grade 4+ Grade 2 only requires natural minor. Memorise it now; the others build on it. Trick: A natural minor = the white notes from A to A. C major = the white notes from C to C. They share all notes — they're relative . Every major key has a relative minor a minor 3rd (3 semitones) below. Memorise this pairing now: it saves hours later. Chapter 3 — Dotted rhythms A dot after a note adds half its value : 1 2 3 ♩. = ♩ + ♪ (dotted crotchet = crotchet + quaver = 1.5 beats) ♪. = ♪ + 𝅘𝅥𝅯 (dotted quaver = quaver + semiquaver = 0.75 beats) The Grade 2 staple is the dotted-quaver + semiquaver pair: 1 2 ♪. 𝅘𝅥𝅯 = 3/4 beat + 1/4 beat ( one beat total ) Count subdivisions: 1 2 3 1 -e-&- a ( 4 semiquavers = 1 beat) [long ] [s] (dotted- q on "1-e-&" , semiq on "a" ) Trick: I subdivided in semiquavers aloud for every dotted pair for 2 weeks: "ONE-e-and-AH, ONE-e-and-AH". Sounds ridiculous, locks the ratio in. Once it's automatic, drop the speaking. Bow distribution for dotted rhythms The long note gets more bow , the short note gets less . Roughly 3:1 ratio matching the duration: 1 2 3 dotted -quaver: 3 inches of bow semiquaver : 1 inch of bow If you give them equal bow, the short note sounds louder (more bow speed in less time). Wrong feel. Chapter 4 — Longer slurs and bow planning Grade 1 slurs were 2–4 notes. Grade 2 introduces 6, 8, even a full scale (8 notes) on one bow. The bow-budget rule Total bow length = ~25 inches (varies by player + bow). For 8 notes in one bow: 25 ÷ 8 ≈ 3 inches per note. You cannot play loud + slow + long-slurred. Pick two. Grade 2 long slurs are usually mezzo-piano and steady — the bow conserves itself. Slur with string crossing Example: slur "open A → 1st finger B → open E" in one bow. Two string changes inside one stroke. The right wrist + elbow tilt to roll between strings without breaking the sound. Where I got stuck: every slur with a string crossing scratched on the crossing point. Fix: slow practice with the metronome at 40 bpm, paying attention to the angle of the bow hair at the crossing. The bow should tilt gradually, not snap. Drill: 5 minutes a day for 2 weeks → solved. Practice progression 2-note slur , same string. 2-note slur, crossing strings . 4-note slur , same string. 4-note slur, crossing strings . 8-note slur = full scale. Don't jump steps. Each stage takes about a week. Chapter 5 — Intervals (Grade 2 theory) Grade 2 theory paper introduces interval size within the major and natural minor keys: Size Example (C major) Notes spanned 2nd C–D 2 3rd C–E 3 4th C–F 4 5th C–G 5 6th C–A 6 7th C–B 7 8ve C–C (high) 8 Trick: count letter names inclusive . C to E = C, D, E = 3 letters = a 3rd. Never count semitones for size at Grade 2 — that's Grade 3 (interval quality). Practise: pick a key, name every interval from the tonic. Then play each on the violin. Linking name + sound + hand position triples retention. Chapter 6 — Suggested Practice Pieces Suzuki Vol. 2 staples Piece Composer Why Chorus from Judas Maccabeus Handel First taste of "real" Baroque tone shaping Musette Bach (arr.) Dance rhythm, slurred phrases Hunters' Chorus C. M. von Weber Two-string passages; energetic Long, Long Ago (Tempo di Minuetto) Bayly Two-octave reach Waltz Brahms First waltz; bow distribution challenge Bourrée Handel Compound dotted rhythms Two Grenadiers Schumann Strong dotted-march rhythm Theme from Witches' Dance Paganini Suzuki's "shock" piece; first time you feel virtuoso ABRSM Grade 2 alternatives Piece Composer Why Minuet in D Mozart (attr.) Classical phrasing Aria Tchaikovsky Lyrical line; bow control test Polka Czech traditional Quick string crossings Listening assignment Watch a recording of Itzhak Perlman or Hilary Hahn playing Bach Partita No. 2 — Allemande (don't try to play it; just listen). Notice how each note has identical bow weight despite enormous variety in speed. That's the Grade 2 goal: even tone across changes. Chapter 7 — Intonation upgrade: cross-string checking Grade 1 used drones on open strings. Grade 2 adds two-string checks at the same pitch: Pitch Way 1 Way 2 A4 Open A 3rd finger on D E5 Open E 3rd finger on A D5 3rd finger on A (also = open string interval check) If the two ways give the same pitch , you're in tune. If they fight, one finger is off. Trick: end every scale with a check-note. Play G major scale up to G5, then immediately play open G and the G5 together as a double-stop. If the octave rings, your top note is true. If it beats, adjust. Tape removal If you used tape on the fingerboard in Grade 1, remove it by Grade 2 exam. The eyes-on-fingerboard habit costs you sight-reading speed. Chapter 8 — Aural / Listening Skills ABRSM Grade 2 aural adds: Clap back rhythm in 6/8 (new at Grade 2). Sing back a 4-bar phrase. Identify if a melody is in major or minor. Identify the time signature (2/4, 3/4, 4/4, or 6/8 ). Major vs minor identification Major = "bright, happy". Minor = "sad, darker". The most reliable test: the third . Major 3rd (C–E) = 4 semitones. Minor 3rd (C–E♭) = 3 semitones. Trick: sing "Happy Birthday" (major) immediately, then "Hey Jude" verse (also major) — internalise the colour . Then sing "Greensleeves" (Dorian, sounds minor) or "House of the Rising Sun" (minor) — feel the gloom . After a week of A/B comparisons, you'll identify them in 2 seconds. Chapter 9 — Common Grade 2 Pitfalls Pitfall Fix Low 1 (B♭, F♮) lands at normal 1 position Mark for first week; physical drill Bow runs out before slur ends Bow-budget rule; mark "mp" in pencil to save hair Dotted rhythm becomes triplet (long-short-short instead of long-short) Subdivide in semiquavers aloud Scratching on slurred string crossing Slow practice, watch the hair angle C major fingering forgotten Drill C major scale daily for 2 weeks Eyes stuck on fingerboard Cover with a small towel during scale practice Useful Shortcut Cheat-sheet What How Two-octave G major G string → D string → A string → E string (up to G5) C major weirdness Half-step between 1 and 2 on D string (not 2-3) F major / B♭ "Low 1" on A string A natural minor Same notes as C major, starts on A Dotted-quaver + semiquaver Long:short = 3:1 in duration AND bow Long slur bow budget Divide bow length by note count; save weight Relative minor 3 semitones below the major (C maj ↔ A min) Cross-string intonation check Same-name notes on two strings should match exactly Daily routine (35 min) Block Time Content Tune + 5th check 2 min Tuner + double-stop Bow warm-up 5 min Long open bows + 8-note slurs on each string Scale 8 min Two-octave today's key + arpeggio + relative minor Sight-read 4 min New 8-bar piece in the week's key Repertoire 14 min Current piece, slow → tempo Cool-down 2 min Air-shake bow arm, release tension Suggested listening (context) Piece Performer Why Suzuki Vol. 2 Hilary Hahn (Suzuki recordings) Hear every piece pro-played Concerto in A minor Vivaldi / Anne-Sophie Mutter Standard concerto study piece (Grade 4-5) — listen now for inspiration Méditation from Thaïs Massenet / Joshua Bell Single long line, perfect for studying bow distribution Liebesleid Kreisler Waltz, sentimental, shows dotted rhythm in expressive setting References ABRSM (current). Music Theory in Practice — Grade 2 . ABRSM (current). Violin Exam Pieces — Grade 2 . Suzuki, S. Suzuki Violin School , Vol. 2. Simon Fischer, Basics — Sections 1–3 (still relevant). entry.title: Violin Notes — 01 · Grade 1 First Steps & Repertoire
entry.content: Grade 1 ABRSM violin is where fingers meet strings. The syllabus is small but the techniques inside are foundational: 1st position fingering, three major keys (G, D, A), one-octave scales, basic bowing (détaché and slur), and a handful of short pieces that you'll remember decades later. Series map: 00 Beginner → 01 Grade 1 (this post) → 02 Grade 2 → … → 08 Grade 8. Learning Outcome Place fingers 1, 2, 3, 4 in 1st position on all four strings. Play one-octave scales of G, D, A majors (separate bows). Play one-octave arpeggios for the same keys. Read fluently in treble clef across the first 1.5 octaves above Middle C. Use détaché (separate) bowing cleanly. Begin to feel "in tune" — recognise when a finger placement is sharp or flat. Play 3–5 Grade 1 / Initial Grade pieces with hands together. Chapter 1 — 1st Position fingering What "1st position" means The position number tells you where the first finger sits on the fingerboard. In 1st position , the index finger sits just below the nut — about a whole tone above the open string. From there, fingers 2, 3, 4 extend up the fingerboard, each roughly a whole tone apart (with one half-step adjustment per scale). The diagram shows the A/D major pattern : whole-step between every finger. In other keys, the half-step location shifts (Chapter 3). Finger numbering Finger Number Index 1 Middle 2 Ring 3 Little (pinky) 4 (Thumb supports underneath, no number) — This is opposite to piano — there, the thumb is 1. On the violin, the thumb has no number because it never stops a string; its job is to brace the neck. Trick: coming from piano, I kept calling my thumb "finger 1" and reaching with my index expecting it to be "2". The fix: every Grade 1 piece marks "1" above the index. Trust the printed number, not your old habit. Placing fingers cleanly Fingertip down , not the pad — the smaller contact area produces a cleaner stop. Curved finger — knuckles bent. Just enough pressure to stop the string vibrating above the finger. Too much pressure = sharp pitch + finger fatigue. Drop and lift — don't slide. Vertical motion only. Where I got stuck: I pressed every finger too hard for two months. My left hand cramped after 10 minutes. The fix: deliberately under-press until the note buzzes; then add the minimum extra pressure to stop the buzz. That's the right amount. Most students press 2-3× more than needed. Chapter 2 — Tuning revisited (the violinist's ear) You learnt to tune in Post 00. Grade 1 adds double-stop tuning — bow two adjacent open strings together and listen for the perfect 5th. How a perfect 5th sounds When two strings tuned a perfect 5th apart sound together, the combined tone is smooth and ringing . When slightly off, you hear beats — a wobbling, rough pulse like an out-of-sync washing machine. To tune by 5ths: Tune A to A=440 with a tuner. Bow A and D together gently. Adjust D's fine tuner until beats vanish. Bow D and G together. Adjust G. Bow A and E together. Adjust E. Trick: sit in a quiet room. Beats are easier to hear without background noise. After 6 months of tuning by 5ths, you'll do it automatically — and you'll have built a perfect-5th template in your ear that helps every interval recognition exercise. Chapter 3 — The three Grade 1 scales G major (one octave, G string + D string) Open G → 1st finger A → 2nd finger B → 3rd finger C → open D → 1st finger E → 2nd finger F♯ → 3rd finger G. 1 2 3 G string: G 1 =A 2 =B 3 =C D string: D 1 =E 2 =F♯ 3 =G Half-step location: between finger 2 and finger 3 on each string. (B→C and F♯→G are half-steps.) D major (one octave, D string + A string) Open D → 1 E → 2 F♯ → 3 G → open A → 1 B → 2 C♯ → 3 D. 1 2 3 D string: D 1 =E 2 =F♯ 3 =G A string: A 1 =B 2 =C♯ 3 =D Half-step location: between finger 2 and finger 3 again. A major (one octave, A string + E string) Open A → 1 B → 2 C♯ → 3 D → open E → 1 F♯ → 2 G♯ → 3 A. 1 2 3 A string: A 1 =B 2 =C♯ 3 =D E string: E 1 =F♯ 2 =G♯ 3 =A Same half-step pattern. Trick: G, D, A majors all use the same finger pattern in 1st position: 0-1-2-3 with the half-step between 2 and 3 on each string. Memorise one hand shape; transfer to all three keys. This is the "violin equivalent" of the piano's W-W-H-W-W-W-H — but expressed as finger placement. Arpeggios (Grade 1) The tonic triad spelled out: root, third, fifth, octave. 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 G major arpeggio : G B D G D B G (open) ( 2 ) (open) ( 3 ) (open) ( 2 ) (open) G str G str D str D str D str G str G str D major arpeggio : D F ♯ A D A F ♯ D A major arpeggio : A C ♯ E A E C ♯ A Practise scales and arpeggios in pairs: G major scale → G major arpeggio → G again. Builds the key-feel. Chapter 4 — Bowing: détaché and slur Détaché "Detached" — each note gets its own bow stroke (down or up). The bow doesn't lift between notes; it changes direction on the string. In Grade 1 you play almost everything détaché . Goal: smooth, even tone with no scratching at the bow direction change. The wrist makes a tiny "give" at each change, like a pendulum bottom. Slur A curved line over two or more notes means play them in one bow stroke (one direction, no change). Same hair, multiple finger changes. 1 2 3 ♪ ♪ ( no slur) = two separate bows: down-up ♪‿♪ (slurred) = one bow stroke, both notes Where I got stuck: I scratched every bow change for the first 2 months. Fix: practise the bow change motion itself without a string — just air bow with the empty bow, smoothly reversing direction. The wrist learns to soften the change. Then add the string back. Bow distribution On a slur of 4 notes, you have to "ration" the bow length so you don't run out. Roughly: divide the bow into 4 equal parts; one part per note. Practice: slur 2 notes per bow, then 4, then 8. By Grade 3 you'll be slurring entire scales in one bow. Chapter 5 — Reading music for violin Violin reads in treble clef only (unlike the piano, which uses both). Range covers from open G (below the staff, on a ledger line) up to many ledger lines above. By Grade 1 you read up to about A or B above the staff (3rd finger on E string). Notes you'll meet in Grade 1 Note Where on violin G3 Open G string (lowest) A3 1 on G B3 2 on G C4 3 on G D4 Open D E4 1 on D F♯4 2 on D G4 3 on D A4 Open A B4 1 on A C♯5 2 on A D5 3 on A E5 Open E F♯5 1 on E G♯5 2 on E A5 3 on E (top note Grade 1) Trick: when sight-reading a Grade 1 piece, mark the string and finger above each note in pencil for the first read. After 3 plays through, erase the markings — your hand has memorised the pattern. By the end of Grade 1 you should be doing this in your head, not on paper. Chapter 6 — Suggested Practice Pieces These pieces match Grade 1 / Initial Grade. Most are in Suzuki Violin School Vol. 1 or freely available on IMSLP. Suzuki Vol. 1 staples (Grade 1 level) Piece Composer / Source Why Twinkle Variations Suzuki arr. The canonical first piece. Same melody, 5 bowing variations. Teaches bow control by rhythm Lightly Row German folk Open-string-heavy, simple finger work Song of the Wind German folk Tests left-hand independence early Go Tell Aunt Rhody American folk Slow, beautiful, teaches singing tone O Come, Little Children German folk Two-string crossings, simple May Song German folk First feel of dance-rhythm Long, Long Ago T. H. Bayly Lyrical; first time you'll want to add vibrato (resist until Grade 3) Allegro Suzuki Energetic; tests détaché bowing speed ABRSM Grade 1 alternatives Piece Composer Why Minuet No. 1 in G Bach (attr.) Classical entry; same tune as piano students play Russian Dance Various Folk dance feel, simple Lavender's Blue English folk Lyrical, classic How to study a piece Listen to a recording 3 times before touching the violin. Sight-read pizzicato (pluck the strings) — checks left-hand alone before the bow complicates it. Bow slowly — 1/4 of target tempo with metronome. Hands together at tempo — only once you can play each separately without thinking. Memorise the first 4 bars by week 1. Trick: always say note names aloud as you play during slow practice. The voice + hand link locks the note-name-to-pitch connection. Later you'll do this silently, but the verbal pass is the cement. Chapter 7 — Intonation: the violin's hardest problem Unlike piano (perfect pitch every key), violin pitch depends entirely on where your finger lands . Even 1 millimetre off = audibly out of tune. How to develop intonation Listen to open strings constantly. Cross-check stopped notes against open strings of the same name. Drone practice. Bow an open string, then play a scale on the next string. The open string is your reference; stopped notes that match the harmonic ring are in tune. Use ear-training apps. "Tonal Energy", "Functional Ear Trainer". Sing the note first , then play it. Singing pre-tunes your hand. Where I got stuck: I couldn't tell if I was sharp or flat — everything sounded "kind of right". Fix: bow the open A while pressing 3rd finger on D (which should match A). If the two pitches fight — beats appear — I was off. If they fuse into one ringing tone — in tune. After a month of drone practice, my finger landed correctly without conscious thought. Tape on the fingerboard (controversial but works) Many teachers put small pieces of tape across the fingerboard at the 1st, 3rd, and 4th finger positions for absolute beginners. Provides a visual guide for finger placement. Pros: speeds up first 3 months; reduces frustration. Cons: trains eyes-on-fingerboard habit; must be removed by Grade 2 or it becomes a crutch. Use it if you're self-teaching and frustrated. Remove it as soon as you can hit the notes without looking. By Grade 1 exam, no tape. Chapter 8 — Aural / Listening Skills ABRSM Grade 1 violin aural is identical to piano aural at Grade 1: Clap back a 2-bar rhythm in 2/4, 3/4, or 4/4. Sing back a 3-4 note phrase. Identify the time signature by listening to a tune. Violin-specific aural exercise Match pitch — examiner plays a note on the piano; you play it on the violin. Tests pitch perception + finger placement under pressure. Tuning judgment — examiner plays two notes; you say which is higher or whether they're the same. Trick: practise pitch matching daily for 60 seconds. Pick a random note on a piano (or use a tuning app), then find it on your violin. By Grade 1 exam you should hit within a quarter-tone first try. Chapter 9 — Common Grade 1 Pitfalls Pitfall Fix Finger lands but is flat (too low) The half-step between 2-3 means 3 is close to 2. Beginners leave too much space. Tape or drone-check Scratching on bow change Wrist softens the change; slow practice with only bow change drill Squeezing the bow Fingers curved + relaxed. Test: can you wiggle them slightly while bowing? If no, you're squeezing Looking at fingers, not music Cover the fingerboard with a small towel for one passage. Force eyes onto the staff Tuning by guess Always tuner-first the first 6 months. Ear comes with practice in tune, not from guessing Practising for too long 20-25 min focused beats 45 min tense.
